abstract: Adaptive mutations in one (home) environment often have diverse effects in other (non-home) environments. This so-called pleiotropy has important implications for the ability of populations to survive environmental fluctuations, which are common in nature. But how the fitness effects vary across mutations, genetic backgrounds and environments is poorly characterized empirically, and a unifying theory describing this variation is lacking. To address this gap, we develop the so-called global epistasis family of models and find that it explains a substantial proportion of variation in the distributions of mutational effects across genetic backgrounds and environments in a published yeast dataset. We then examine evolutionary dynamics that emerge in this model and we find that, as a population adapts at home, its non-home fitness can either converge to an intermediate finite value, or increase or decline indefinitely, with the empirical parameters being consistent with the first two outcomes. This work provides a quantitative unification of pleiotropy and epistasis, generates testable predictions for the pleiotropic consequences of adaptation and enables a better understanding of evolution in fluctuating environments.
